claims.text: The starting material consists of crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
Forming a multi-principal-element alloy introduces high configurational entropy.
Introducing high configurational entropy can stabilize the structure of near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
The proposed stabilization applies during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
High configurational entropy lowers the Gibbs free energy of the solid solution.
Lowering the solid-solution Gibbs free energy stabilizes the host matrix against sintering.
High configurational entropy promotes catalyst self-regeneration.
The intervention will improve nanoparticle stability and sintering resistance relative to nanoparticles without introduced high configurational entropy.
The proposed boundary includes thermal exposures lasting several hours to days.
The exact stabilization mechanism is not fully understood.
TEM or SEM can be used to measure nanoparticle size and shape before and after thermal exposure.
XRD or XPS can be used to assess nanoparticle composition before and after thermal exposure.
Significant sintering or compositional change after exposure would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The starting nanoparticles are already defined as near-equiatomic solid solutions of five or more metals, which ordinarily constitutes a multi-principal-element, configurationally entropic alloy. Consequently, forming such an alloy is not clearly a new intervention, and a baseline described as the same nanoparticles without introduced configurational entropy is not operationally distinguishable.
